newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia's ARS gem group to raise foreign financing.
newsitem.headline: Russia's ARS gem group to raise foreign financing.

text.p: Almazy Rossii-Sakha (ARS) -- Russia's dominant diamond producer and a lynchpin in global gem markets -- aims to begin tapping world financial sources this year, ARS Vice-President Syemyon Zelberg said.

"The company's key task in 1997 is to attract medium-term credit -- we have things in which to invest the money," he told Reuters in a brief interview at the weekend in the Siberian city of Mirny, where the company is based.
ARS is looking at a range of options, including syndicated credits with a Western banking consortium, Eurobond issues and share issues on Canadian stock markets via an ARS subsidiary.

Once a long-delayed gem deal with De Beers of South Africa is approved by Moscow, ARS plans to sign a syndicated credit of around $500 million over three years with a group of Western banks led by Britain's National Westminster.

First Deputy Prime Minister Anatoly Chubais said last week that the long-delayed export agreement would be signed no later than June 4. He also said that a decree outlining diamond export quotas for the whole year should also be signed by then.
The government recently signed a decree outlining exports to the end of May. Until that document was passed, ARS had exported practically nothing this year.
Company sources said ARS would export no less than $550 million worth of diamonds annually through De Beers under the gem export deal with the South African giant.
De Beers sharply curtailed purchases of ARS diamonds at the end of last year when Moscow failed to make its position clear on a draft agreement submitted to the cabinet in October 1996.

De Beers' London-based Central Selling Organisation controls about three quarters of the world's $4.5 billion-a-year trade in uncut diamonds, and Russia accounts for about 20 percent of annual CSO sales.
Zelberg said that ARS planned to issue Eurobonds at the end of this year worth $100 million and aimed to boost earnings from the issues by $300 million a year.

The company also wants to issue shares in its subsidiary ARS-Nyurba on Canadian stock markets to finance development of new diamond-bearing kimberlite deposits. Zelberg said the planned share issue in Canada was already fairly "advanced" and could take place later this year.

"We have to carry out a detailed geological assessment on these (kimberlite) pipes this year or next and build a large mineral enriching plant to do this," Zelberg said. "We need around $500 million to do so."
ARS representatives said that attracting investment was the key to boosting diamond production and maintaining the firm's near-monopoly position in Russia.

ARS press spokesman Yuri Beskakotov quoted ARS President Vyacheslav Shtyrov as saying during a meeting with Chubais in Mirny last week that the company aimed to increase diamond production by 30 percent over five years.
But to do so, the company would have to raise at least $300 million in extra funds in addition to its own investment resources, he quoted Shtyrov as saying.
ARS sold $1.44 billion of gems in 1996, up from $1.35 billion in 1995. Its 35 divisions employ 36,000 people.

ARS has unmined reserves worth $40 billion, half of which can be developed by open-cast mining methods, Beskakotov said. The reserves are sufficient to guarantee production at planned levels until 2050.
Beskakotov said ARS did not want the Russian government to intervene in its plans. "We ask one thing from the government -- that they do not meddle in our activities," he said.
The company's largest shareholders are the State Property Fund and the Sakha Republic State Property Fund, each with 32 percent. Employees own 23 percent.
